paper_title: QuadTok: Quadtree Visual Tokenizer for Autoregressive Image Generation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: We introduce QuadTok, a novel framework for visual tokenization and autoregressive image generation. Compared to traditional approaches using 2D grids or 1D token sequences, we propose a hierarchical quadtree structure, bridging the gap between 2D spatial binding and 1D sequence-level flexibility. The QuadTok tokenizer dynamically allocates representational capacity to visually intricate areas while leaving homogeneous regions at a coarse resolution. Compared with a fixed 256-token grid, our ImageNet-trained tokenizer saves approximately 10% of tokens on ImageNet and 9% when transferred zero-shot to the COCO dataset, while maintaining comparable reconstruction fidelity. Furthermore, the natural causality introduced by the tree structure seamlessly enables autoregressive image generation. Conditioned on a quadtree topology supplied before generation, our 947M GPT-style generative model achieves a 2.08 gFID on the ImageNet $256 \times 256$ benchmark. Additionally, leveraging the strong spatial correlation preserved by the quadtree structure, the QuadTok generator enables zero-shot spatially controlled image generation capabilities. Code: https://github.com/myc634/QuadTok.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Natural images exhibit highly non-uniform spatial information density: regions containing intricate textures and high-frequency patterns carry significantly more information than smooth or homogeneous areas. Ideally, visual tokenizer should allocate representational capacity according to this 1 Preprint. spatial variability. However, classic visual tokenizers (van den Oord et al., 2018; Sun et al., 2024) compress images into rigid 2D grids with fixed token budget, distributing tokens uniformly across the image regardless of local complexity. As result, complex regions are often under-represented while simple regions are over-allocated with redundant tokens. To overcome the rigidity of grid-based tokenization, recent work has explored 1D visual tokenizers (Shen et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2024b; Duggal et al., 2024; Miwa et al., 2025b; Wang et al., 2026; Bachmann et al., 2025b; Chen et al., 2026). These methods model images as sequential token streams and allow for variable length, offering greater flexibility in adapting the token budget to image complexity. Nevertheless, this flexibility comes at the cost of spatial awareness. Because token allocation occurs along the sequence dimension rather than the image plane, these approaches remain largely spatially agnostic. Consequently, they often lack explicit correspondence between tokens and image patches, which can degrade pixel-level fidelity and make them less suitable for downstream tasks that require spatially grounded representations and precise localization. In this work, we propose QuadTok, novel quadtree-based visual tokenizer that enables adaptive token allocation while preserving explicit spatial correspondence. Instead of relying on rigid grid or purely sequential representation, QuadTok represents images using hierarchical quadtree structure that dynamically subdivides spatial regions based on local complexity. This design bridges the gap between existing paradigms: it retains the spatial grounding of traditional 2D tokenizers while introducing the sequence-level flexibility of 1D token representations. However, one key challenge remains: How can we select which regions to refine based on their reconstruction benefit? To tackle this, we propose Region-Wise Complexity Guidance, data-driven strategy to select content-adaptive tree for each image based on reconstruction benefit. Furthermore, we identify that maintaining the hierarchical causality and explicit spatial relationships between tree nodes is crucial during the tokenization process. To enforce this structural integrity, we introduce the Kinship Causal Mask. This mechanism dictates strict coarse-to-fine information flow along the quadtree hierarchy, allowing the global image structure to be established before localized refinement occurs within spatially bounded regions. Empowered by our Region-Wise Complexity Guidance, the QuadTok tokenizer achieves an rFID of 1.46 and PSNR of 20.37 on ImageNet with 230 tokens on average, saving approximately 10% relative to fixed 256-token grid. Transferred zero-shot to COCO, the same tokenizer uses 232 tokens on average, saving approximately 9%. Furthermore, leveraging the causality inherent in the quadtree structure, the QuadTok 947M autoregressive generator achieves gFID of 2.08, compared with 2.15 for the 1.4B RandAR-XXL model (Pang et al., 2025). We also show consistent scaling behavior on our generator across different model scales. Furthermore, guided by the explicit quadtree topology, QuadTok generator enables novel zero-shot capabilities such as spatially controllable generation. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We propose QuadTok, quadtree-based visual tokenizer that replaces fixed-grid representations with spatially adaptive token allocation. Our approach preserves explicit spatial correspondence while enabling flexible token budgets driven by local visual complexity. We introduce two key mechanisms to support adaptive tokenization: (i) Region-Wise Complexity Guidance strategy selecting regional refinement from reconstruction benefit; (ii) Kinship Causal Mask enforcing hierarchical dependencies among tree nodes during tokenization. Leveraging the hierarchical causality of quadtrees, QuadTok achieves competitive image generation quality while enabling zero-shot spatially controllable image synthesis conditioned on quadtree layouts supplied before generation.

sections.title: 2.1 VISUAL TOKENIZATION
sections.content: Visual tokenizers compress images into representations for generative modeling. VQ-VAE (van den Oord et al., 2018) learns discrete codebooks, and VQ-GAN (Esser et al., 2021) adds adversarial training to improve perceptual reconstruction. Later work improves codebook design and tokenizer architectures (Lee et al., 2022; Mentzer et al., 2024; Yu et al., 2024a; Zhao et al., 2024). Beyond fixed spatial grids, TiTok (Yu et al., 2024b) represents images as compact 1D sequences. FlexTok (Bachmann et al., 2025a) and One-D-Piece (Miwa et al., 2025b) support variable sequence lengths, while GigaTok (Xiong et al., 2025) uses semantic regularization to improve reconstruction 2 Preprint. and downstream generation as tokenizers scale. QuadTok focuses on assigning discrete tokens to regions within an image while retaining an explicit spatial correspondence. Content-adaptive tokenization. CAT (Shen et al., 2025) adapts representation capacity to image complexity by using caption-derived scores to select an image-wide compression ratio in nested continuous VAE. Its variable-length latents support image synthesis with diffusion transformer. QuadTok instead allocates discrete tokens at different spatial resolutions within each image, preserving explicit correspondence between tokens and regions. During reconstruction, image content determines which regions to refine; during generation, an autoregressive model predicts visual codes under topology supplied before sampling. We compare with CATs published ImageNet 512 512 generation results in Tab. 7, alongside other high-resolution generators.

sections.title: 2.2 AUTOREGRESSIVE IMAGE GENERATION
sections.content: Autoregressive image models differ in both their latent representation and prediction unit (Lee et al., 2022; Li et al., 2024; Shan et al., 2026). LlamaGen (Sun et al., 2024) predicts discrete grid tokens sequentially, RandAR (Pang et al., 2025) changes their generation order, and VAR (Tian et al., 2024) predicts successive resolution scales. DPAR (Srivastava et al., 2025) uses an entropy model to group discrete tokens into variable-length patches, reducing the sequence processed by its global transformer. We compare with DPAR as related approach to spatial token aggregation. QuadTok represents regions directly as quadtree nodes and generates their discrete codes in breadth-first order conditioned on the given tree. Continuous-token methods provide another approach to autoregressive synthesis. xAR (Ren et al., 2025a) generalizes the prediction unit to entities such as cells and uses flow matching with noisy contexts. FlowAR (Ren et al., 2025b) combines scale-wise autoregression with flow matching. QuadTok models variable-length discrete sequences with explicit regional correspondence, allowing generation to be conditioned on supplied spatial topology.

sections.title: 2.3 QUADTREE REPRESENTATIONS IN VISION
sections.content: Quadtrees recursively partition two-dimensional space and have been used for image processing, compression, and adaptive visual computation (Wu, 2018; Tang et al., 2022; Ronen et al., 2023; Its Zhao et al., 2025). QuadTok incorporates this hierarchy into generative visual tokenizer. topology-aware attention preserves structured interactions among tokens, and its discrete representation supports image reconstruction and autoregressive synthesis under supplied spatial topology.

sections.title: 3.1 QUADTOK TOKENIZER
sections.content: We introduce QuadTok, visual tokenizer that represents images using an adaptive quadtree structure. Unlike conventional methods that rely on fixed grids, QuadTok dynamically allocates tokens across regions while maintaining explicit correspondence between tokens and the image patches.

sections.title: 3.1.1 QUADTREE REPRESENTATION
sections.content: QuadTok represents an image using hierarchical quadtree decomposition, where each node corresponds to spatial region and is treated as visual token. node is defined by the attribute tuple (l, p), where denotes the tree level and the spatial index. Level = 1 represents coarse regions of the image, while level = 2 corresponds to higher-resolution subdivisions. Each parent node may expand into four child nodes covering its spatial quadrants. Our default configuration uses two levels; we also evaluate three-level extension in Secs. 4.1 and 4.2. To interface this hierarchical structure with Transformer architecture, the quadtree is serialized into 1D sequence using breadth-first search (BFS) traversal. This ordering first lists all coarse tokens and then their corresponding higher-resolution child tokens, naturally aligning with coarse-to-fine generation. 3.1.

sections.title: 3.1.4 HIERARCHICAL DECODING
sections.content: To reconstruct the image from the discrete token sequence, we reverse the tokenization process through coarse-to-fine hierarchical decoding procedure. The discrete tokens are first mapped back to continuous embeddings using the codebook and combined with their corresponding structural instruction embeddings. For token associated with node (li, pi), we have zi = eyi + qi where eyi denotes the embedding of the discrete token index and qi is the node instruction embedding encoding the tree level and spatial position. Transformer-based Decoder then processes the embedding sequence as = [z1, , zM ]. Unlike standard grid-based decoders that directly reshape the output sequence into dense spatial grid, QuadTok reconstructs the image according to the quadtree hierarchy. Each processed node feature zi is first projected into spatial patch using level-specific projection module: Cli(pi) = Uli(zi) where Ul() denotes the unpatching operator for level l, producing spatial feature patch corresponding to region p. The patches from the same level are placed at their corresponding spatial locations on canvas to form residual feature map Cl. We then aggregate the feature map level-by-level as Hl+1 = up l+1 is learned upsampling module for level + 1. l+1(Hl) + Cl+1 where H0 = 0, and up 4 Preprint. This process starts with coarse global representation using level-1 tokens and then progressively refines local details using higher resolution tokens. sections.title: 3.2 KINSHIP CAUSAL ATTENTION
sections.content: Flattening the quadtree into 1D sequence removes the explicit hierarchical constraints of the original structure. Without additional restrictions, standard self-attention would allow tokens to interact globally, potentially breaking the spatial correspondence between tokens and their associated image regions. To preserve the hierarchical topology, we introduce Kinship Causal Attention, topologyaware masking strategy that constrains attention according to the quadtree structure. During encoding, the Aggregator Transformer processes the concatenated sequence [F Q] of ViT feature tokens and quadtree instruction tokens Q. Attention is asymmetric: ViT tokens attend bidirectionally among themselves, and quadtree tokens attend to all ViT tokens, but not vice versa. Tree tokens thus draw on globally contextualized image features, while their region and level embeddings specify the regions they represent. During decoding, the Decoder Transformer processes the quantized visual tokens together with their corresponding quadtree instruction tokens. In both the encoding and decoding stages, the selfattention interactions among quadtree tokens are governed by our proposed Kinship Causal Mask, which enforces strict coarse-to-fine dependency consistent with the quadtree hierarchy. This mask is used within the tokenizer, whereas the autoregressive generator uses standard causal mask over the BFS token sequence. For the two-level tokenizer, the Kinship Causal Mask follows three structural rules: Parent Parent. Coarse-level tokens attend to each other bidirectionally to establish the global image layout. Child Parent. Fine-level tokens attend to all parent tokens to obtain global structural context, while parent tokens are prevented from attending to child tokens. Child Sibling. Fine-level tokens attend only to other child tokens that share the same parent node, restricting refinement within each spatial region. Fig. 3 illustrates the two-level pattern. The same rule extends to deeper trees: node can attend to all nodes at coarser levels and to siblings sharing its immediate parent at the same level, but not to finer-level nodes. The coarsest level retains full bidirectional attention. Thus, level-3 nodes attend to all level-1 and level-2 nodes and bidirectionally to their level-3 siblings. These constraints impose coarse-to-fine flow and restrict same-level interactions among tree tokens to siblings. The ablation in Sec. 4.4.1 evaluates their effect on reconstruction and generation.

sections.title: 3.4 QUADTREE-BASED AUTOREGRESSIVE IMAGE GENERATION
sections.content: Given quadtree structure supplied before generation, we synthesize its visual token sequence = [y1, , yM ] autoregressively: p(Y c, ) = (cid:81)M i=1 p(yiy<i, c, ti) where denotes the conditioning signal (e.g. class label) and ti = (li, pi) represents the tree attributes of node i. The topology is selected before sampling, but node instructions are presented in BFS order. At step i, the model can use only the current and preceding node instructions, not future nodes. We parameterize this distribution using LLaMA (Touvron et al., 2023)-style decoder-only Transformer with standard causal attention mask. Each visual-token prediction depends only on preceding visual codes and the supplied conditioning information; the tokenizers bidirectional parent and sibling interactions are not used in the generator. Structural instruction embeddings encode the quadtree geometry, which specifies both the tree level and spatial position of each token, enabling the model to condition generation on spatial hierarchy. During inference, tokens are generated sequentially in BFS order. Coarse tokens appear first, establishing the global structure, after which finer tokens progressively refine local details and textures. The generator predicts visual codes under the supplied topology, enabling layout-controlled synthesis from user-defined or algorithmically constructed trees.

sections.title: 4.2 QUADTOK GENERATION
sections.content: Implementation Details. QuadTok uses decoder-only autoregressive generator following LlamaGen (Sun et al., 2024). The two-level generator family comprises 111M (B), 343M (L), 697M (XL), and 947M (XXL) models, and the three-level generator contains 344M parameters. Generation predicts visual codes conditioned on topology specified before sampling. For the unconditional topology setting, we sample random trees independently of the image content to be generated. Generator training and sampling details are provided in Appendix C. IMAGENET GENERATION BENCHMARK.

sections.title:
4.4.1 EFFECTIVENESS OF THE KINSHIP CAUSAL MASK
We ablate the Kinship Causal Mask (Sec. 3.2) by training a baseline QuadTok with unconstrained
bidirectional attention over all flattened tree tokens, and study its effect on spatial correlation, re-
construction, and generation (Tab. 4).
sections.content: Spatial correlation. To probe tokenregion binding, we perturb single fine-level token (l=2) with random codebook index and compare the perturbed and unperturbed reconstructions. With the mask, the resulting difference remains localized to the corresponding spatial patch; without it, the difference spreads across the image. This spatial correspondence supports the zero-shot spatial control in Sec. 4.3. Reconstruction and generation. This spatial isolation is also reflected quantitatively (Tab. 4). Without the mask, the tokenizer degenerates toward sequential 1D code: rFID is slightly lower (1.461.41), but PSNR drops by over point (20.3719.16), trading spatial fidelity for perceptual realism. The gap widens downstream: with the same 697M generator and CFG, removing the mask raises gFID from 2.23 to 3.17, showing that spatially structured tokens matter for AR generation.

sections.title: 4.4.2 REGION-WISE COMPLEXITY GUIDANCE STRATEGY.
sections.content: Does guidance help? We compare quadtree constructions on ImageNet-1K reconstruction (Tab. 5). uniformly expanded (Full) tree reconstructs well but is token-heavy (320), and Random tree of similar size is worse (rFID 1.60 at 253 tokens). Guided by Region-wise Complexity Guidance (Sec. 3.3), QuadTok concentrates tokens on visually complex regions and matches Full fidelity (rFID 1.46, PSNR 20.37) with 28% fewer tokens (230). We adopt LPIPS-based guidance with τ =0.05 as the default; the full probing-metric and threshold ablation is provided in Appendix G.

sections.title: 5 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We present QuadTok, quadtree-based tokenizer that enables spatially adaptive, variable-length visual representations. By organizing tokens in quadtree structure, QuadTok allocates tokens according to local complexity while preserving spatial correspondence between tokens and image regions which bridges adaptive tokenization and structured spatial representations. Experiments show that QuadTok achieves strong reconstruction and generation performance while enabling zero-shot spatial layout control. While this work focuses on class-conditional generation, QuadTok is compatible with multimodal pipelines and text-to-image generation, which we leave for future work. 9 Preprint.

sections.title: B QUADTOK TOKENIZER TRAINING DETAILS
sections.content: We train the QuadTok tokenizer on the ImageNet-1K training set at resolution of 256 256. The Encoder adopts Vision Transformer (ViT) backbone comprising 8x Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017) blocks with patch size of 16 16 and learnable positional embeddings (Heo et al., 2024; Su et al., 2023). The Aggregator and Decoder modules follow similar architecture, each containing 8x Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017) blocks, but we only apply structural instruction embedding instead using standard position embedding widly using in Visiton Transformer. The hidden embedding dimension across all modules is fixed at 512. Following LlamaGen (Sun et al., 2024), we employ shared codebook across all tree levels with vocabulary size = 16384 and latent dimensionality = 8. During training, probabilistic tree sampling is applied with child node expansion probability γ = 0.5, which balances computational efficiency and reconstruction fidelity. The tokenizer contains approximately 120M parameters. For the quadtree structure, we use two depth levels with spatial token grids of 8 8 and 16 16. The unpatched spatial footprint of each token is set to p1 = p2 = 8. The hidden embedding dimension is fixed to 512 across all modules. Following LlamaGen (Sun et al., 2024), we use 14 Preprint. shared codebook across tree levels with vocabulary size = 16384 and latent dimension = 8. During training, probabilistic tree sampling is applied with child expansion probability γ = 0.5, balancing computational efficiency and reconstruction fidelity. In total, the tokenizer contains approximately 120M parameters. To optimize the tokenizer, we employ combination of reconstruction and adversarial objectives. The overall training objective Ltotal is formulated as weighted sum of four distinct loss components: Ltotal = λM SELM SE + λLP IP SLLP IP + λV QLV + λGAN LGAN where LM SE denotes the Mean Squared Error for exact pixel-level fidelity, and LLP IP is the Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity loss, which preserves high-frequency visual details and structural integrity. LV represents the Vector Quantization commitment loss necessary to align the continuous visual representations with the discrete codebook. To further enhance the perceptual realism and sharpness of the reconstructed images, we incorporate an adversarial GAN loss, denoted by LGAN . The hyperparameters λM SE, λLP IP S, λV Q, and λGAN control the relative contribution of each corresponding objective. To ensure initial training stability and proper codebook convergence, the adversarial weight λGAN is strictly set to 0 initially and is only activated after the first 200,000 training steps. For each loss weight, we apply the same setting with (Miwa et al., 2025a)

sections.title: C QUADTOK GENERATOR TRAINING DETAILS
sections.content: The architecture of the QuadTok generator follows the decoder-only Autoregressive(AR) generation paradigm adopted in LlamaGen (Sun et al., 2024). We incorporate several modern architectural components, including Query-Key (QK) Normalization (Henry et al., 2020), SwiGLU activation functions (Shazeer, 2020), and Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE) (Heo et al., 2024). We scale the two-level generator across four model sizes: 111M (B), 343M (L), 697M (XL), and 947M (XXL) parameters. The three-level generator contains 344M parameters. All models are trained for 300 epochs (approximately 360K iterations) using global batch size of 1024, without applying exponential moving average (EMA) to the model weights. Optimization is performed using the AdamW (Kingma & Ba, 2014) optimizer with β1 = 0.9, β2 = 0.95, and weight decay 0.05. The learning rate is set to 4 104 for the first 250 epochs without warm-up, followed by linear decay to 1 105 over the final 50 epochs. To mitigate overfitting and enable Classifier-Free Guidance (Ho & Salimans, 2022b;a) (CFG), the class conditioning embeddings are randomly dropped with probability 0.1 during training. During inference, we employ standard Key-Value (KV) cache to accelerate autoregressive decoding, together with dynamic power-cosine CFG scheduler to improve sample fidelity. key characteristic of our framework is that the quadtree topology must be predefined before generation. Quadtree structure during inference. For class-conditional ImageNet evaluation, we sample quadtree topologies independently of image content using probabilistic expansion policy. Each sampled topology specifies the regions to refine, and its node instructions are presented in breadthfirst order as the generator predicts visual codes. HIGH-RESOLUTION RECONSTRUCTION AND GENERATION We evaluate QuadTok on ImageNet at 512 512 to test whether spatially adaptive tokenization and topology-conditioned generation extend to higher resolution. We retain two quadtree levels and enlarge the spatial grids to 16 16 and 32 32, separating increased image resolution from the deeper-tree experiment. Reconstruction. Region-wise Complexity Guidance allocates tokens according to the reconstruction benefit of refining each region. Tab. 6 compares this allocation with fixed 2D grids and compact 1D tokenizers, demonstrating high-resolution reconstruction with fewer tokens than the 1,024-token grid baselines. Generation. The 344M generator synthesizes native-512 512 images under random topologies supplied before generation. We evaluate 50,000 class-conditional samples using the ImageNet-512 ADM reference. sections.title: F SPATIAL LAYOUT EVALUATION DETAILS
sections.content: We evaluate the frozen two-level ImageNet-trained generator and tokenizer using CFG scale 6, power-cosine guidance schedule with exponent 1, and sampling temperature 1. Each condition contains 20 images for each of 50 fixed ImageNet classes, giving 1,000 images per condition. The four prescribed layouts correspond to the left, right, top, and bottom half-planes. Each topology retains all nodes of an 8 8 coarse grid and expands the 32 cells in the target half-plane, adding four children per cell for total of 192 visual tokens. The matched random baseline uniformly selects exactly 32 coarse cells for expansion independently for each image. Its generated image set is shared across the four directional evaluations. Grad-CAM uses the intended class in ResNet-50. Box localization uses the highest-confidence intended-object box from Grounding DINO, and SAM 2 receives that box as its mask prompt. The Grad-CAM center of mass, box center, or mask centroid is tested against the requested half-plane. Box and mask scores count missed detections as failures and use all generated images as the denominator. FID-50cls compares Inception-v3 features of the 1,000 generated images in each condition with the same 2,500 ImageNet validation images from the 50 evaluated classes. Its value is 35.03 for the random-topology baseline and 35.15, 34.88, 34.97, and 35.05 for the prescribed left, right, top, and bottom layouts, respectively. COMPLEXITY GUIDANCE: METRIC AND THRESHOLD We ablate the probing signal and its expansion threshold τ (Tab. 11), comparing MSE, LPIPS (Zhang et al., 2018), and their linear combination (LMSE 10 + LLPIPS). At matched 230-token budget, LPIPS aligns allocation with perceptual quality better than MSE or the combination (rFID 1.46 vs. 1.67 and 1.58); sweeping τ shows 0.05 best balances token count and fidelity. We therefore adopt LPIPS with τ =0.05 as the default.

sections.title: H LIMITATIONS AND FUTURE WORK
sections.content: While QuadTok demonstrates strong potential in dynamic token allocation and structured autoregressive generation, our current study has two primary limitations. Scale and Modality Constraints. First, due to computational resource limitations, our empirical evaluations are currently confined to class-conditional image generation on the ImageNet dataset. 18 Preprint. Table 11: Ablation of complexity guidance metric and threshold τ . We compare MSE, LPIPS, and their linear combination as probing metrics; for LPIPS we sweep the expansion threshold τ , and report MSE and the combination at matched 230-token budget on ImageNet-1K. LPIPS at τ =0.05 achieves the best perceptual quality (rFID 1.46) at 230 tokens, and is adopted as the default. Guidance Metric Threshold (τ ) #Tokens rFID PSNR LMSE LLPIPS Combined (LMSE 10 + LLPIPS) 0.0005 0.03 0.05 0.06 0.06 230 267 230 195 1.67 1.46 1.46 1.75 1.58 20.52 20.24 20.37 19.99 20. We have not yet scaled the framework to massive, open-domain datasets (e.g., LAION) nor extended the architecture to encompass complex text-to-image synthesis paradigms. Scaling the model capacity and extending the cross-attention mechanisms for open-vocabulary text conditioning require significantly more training compute and represent critical next step. Dataset Bias in Layout Control. Second, the inherent bias of the ImageNet dataset towards objectcentric, single-subject compositions restricts the upper bound of our zero-shot spatial layout control. Although QuadTok effectively localizes primary subjects and separates them from the background based on topological priors, synthesizing highly complex, multi-object scenes with intricate relational layouts remains challenging. The models structural prior is naturally limited by the compositional diversity of its training data. We leave the scaling of QuadTok to large-scale text-to-image generation and its application to scenelevel dataset for complex, multi-object layout control to future work.
